p: Once the trampolines have done their job, Derby has some excellent ways to keep the day going. Markeaton Park, on the north-west side of the city, is a big, popular green space with play areas, a lake and plenty of room for a picnic. Darley Park, on the banks of the Derwent, is another lovely spot for a walk.

Derby Museum and Art Gallery holds a fine collection of paintings by Joseph Wright of Derby, the eighteenth-century artist famous for his dramatic scenes lit by candlelight. It's a great place for a quieter hour after all that noise.

A short drive from the city, Kedleston Hall, cared for by the National Trust, is a grand eighteenth-century mansion with beautiful parkland. Elvaston Castle Country Park, to the south-east, has woodland, a lake and a slightly mysterious Gothic castle, which makes a fun backdrop for a family walk.

Before the bounce, a bit of prep saves faff at the desk. Most trampoline parks want a waiver form filled in, and doing it online first means less queuing. Sporty clothes and a water bottle are all you really need, and a session of around an hour will flatten even the bounciest kids.

If you've got toddlers, look out for sessions aimed at younger children, which tend to be calmer. Older kids and teens might enjoy the more active features, so check what's on at this branch before you book.
Football fans can also pop by Pride Park, home of Derby County, for a look at the stadium.
